title: Bridge Orchestration Sandbox: Authority Matrix, Handoffs, and Customer Message Matrix
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Overview:

This document defines the Bridge Orchestration Sandbox approach: a repeatable, low-friction pattern for temporarily expanding bridge/incident authority, running handoffs, and coordinating customer communications during multi-service incidents. It is intended for on-call operators, incident commanders, bridge operators, support leads, and engineering managers.

Why this exists:
- Reduce handoff friction for rapid containment and stabilization.
- Make who-can-decide explicit (authority matrix) so that escalations are faster and documented.
- Provide ready-to-use customer communication blocks (message matrix) to avoid delays and tone inconsistencies.
- Provide a safe environment ("sandbox") for game-day rehearsals of bridge orchestration without touching production traffic or alerts.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to multi-service availability incidents, SLO regressions, and capacity storms affecting Redwood inference runtime or API layer.
- Not intended for single-service debugging runbooks (use service-specific runbooks in eng-platform or eng-serving-runtime folders).

Key definitions:
- Bridge: A temporary, recorded collaboration channel (Zoom/meet + Slack bridge channel) used for incident coordination.
- Bridge Operator: The person responsible for maintaining the bridge Oracle (agenda, logs, participant list) and publishing status messages.
- Incident Commander (IC): Person with overall decision authority for the incident rally.
- Sandbox: A pre-provisioned staging environment and simulated alerts used for game-days.

Roles and responsibilities (at-a-glance):
- Bridge Operator: open/close bridge, maintain evidence notebook, author status messages. (Primary: on-call SRE; Secondary: support engineer)
- Incident Commander (IC): strategic decisions (customer messaging cadence, rollback vs. mitigation). (Primary: senior SRE or on-call EM)
- Service Lead(s): own technical diagnostic and remediation for their service; provide ETA for fixes.
- Communications Lead (Comms): edits and publishes customer-facing messages. (Primary: customer-success or support)
- Escalation Authority: minority group who can approve immediate cross-team throttles, region failovers, or emergency rollbacks.

Authority matrix (decision lattice):
| Decision type | Default decision owner | Escalation authority | Time-to-decision SLA |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Isolate service / circuit-breaker | Service Lead | IC + Escalation Authority | 10 minutes |
| Region failover activation | IC | CTO / Ops Director | 15 minutes |
| Emergency rollback to prior model | Service Lead + IC | Engineering Director | 20 minutes |
| Customer credit / SLA exception | Comms + Support Lead | Finance Legal approval required within 48h | 24 hours |

Bridge orchestration checklist (immediate actions, first 10 minutes):
1. Acknowledge pager in central tracker and open Bridge (Bridge Operator).
2. IC declares initial severity tier (P0 / P1) and posts public status page placeholder: "We are investigating — more updates shortly."
3. Snapshot critical metrics and alerts: SLO error rate, 95th/99th latency, GPU capacity per cluster, prefix cache eviction rate. Attach links to dashboards.
4. Assign service leads to the bridge. Confirm owners on-call and list contact numbers.
5. If customer-impacting, Comms drafts first external message using Message Matrix.
6. Start evidence collection: traces, recent deploys, config change logs.

Step-by-step bridge orchestration flow (detailed):
- Step 0: Preconditions
  - Sandbox rehearsals completed (see Game-Day section) OR admits to run live bridge.
  - Bridge template (video+Slack channel) created from /templates/bridge-template.
- Step 1: Open bridge and call out goals (Bridge Operator)
  - Statement: "This bridge is to contain and stabilize [service(s)] impacting [customer segment]. Primary goal: stop customer-visible errors. Secondary: identify root cause and mitigation path."
- Step 2: Assign roles (IC announces Service Leads, Recorder, Comms, Safety Officer)
- Step 3: Rapid triage (first 15 minutes)
  - Confirm scope (single-region vs. multi-region).
  - List obvious causes and immediate mitigations (throttle, fallback model, restart pool nodes).
- Step 4: Containment plan (IC + Service Leads)
  - Decide on throttle windows, cache warmers, prefix cache rehydration, or failover schedule. Put actions into the task tracker with owners and ETA.
- Step 5: Stabilize and monitor (after mitigation)
  - Bridge Operator posts a stabilization update with measured metrics showing improvement.
- Step 6: Recovery and closure criteria
  - Recovery defined as 3 consecutive 5-minute windows within SLO targets OR agreed safe fallback (e.g., route to smaller model with acceptable quality).
  - IC closes bridge and publishes an incident summary stub within 2 hours.

Evidence collection matrix (minimum required artifacts):
- Dashboard snapshots (PNG links) for: overall API error rate, latency P95/P99, commit/deploy history, GPU allocation, autoscaler events.
- Logs: representative 5-min logs from affected nodes (redact PII).
- Traces: a sample request trace demonstrating failure pattern.
- Configs: base model version, rollout flags, recent config changes (last 24h).

Customer Message Matrix (blocks to compose external messages quickly):
- Initial customer-facing line (when problem first detected):
  "We are aware of an issue affecting Redwood API responses for some customers. Our engineers are investigating; we will provide an update within 30 minutes."

- Impact clarification options (pick the one that matches):
  - "A subset of customers in [region] may see increased latency or 5xx errors when calling text generation endpoints."
  - "Embed operations may be delayed for affected tenants; existing embeddings remain accessible."
  - "Dedicated customers using reserved pools may see degraded throughput in [cluster-name]."

- Mitigation ETA placeholder: "We are deploying mitigations and expect improvements within X minutes — we will update when we have verified recovery metrics."

- Escalation/credit language (post-incident):
  "We take reliability seriously. If this incident caused production impact for your service, open a support case referencing incident #[INC-ID] and our team will coordinate a post-incident review and any applicable service credits."

Templates (copy-paste ready):
- Public status page (first update):
  "Title: Investigating increased API errors
  Body: We are investigating reports of increased error rates for some API requests. Our engineers have opened a dedicated investigation and we will post a follow-up within 30 minutes. Affected customers: subset in [region]."

- Slack status short (internal):
  "[INC-ID] — Investigating. Bridge: <link>. Service leads: @serviceA, @serviceB. First update in 30m."

Handoff & shift-change checklist (to prevent knowledge loss):
- Outgoing bridge operator posts summary of actions taken, open tasks with owners, and current metrics.
- Incoming operator confirms receipt and repeats back: primary mitigations, next ETA, and any outstanding approvals.
- Document handoff in incident log and update oncall calendar if follow-up tasks cross shifts.

Game-Day sandbox guidance (how to rehearse):
- Frequency: quarterly for critical incident classes (SLO regression, KV cache thrash, multi-region failover).
- Participants: SREs, service owners, CS, Support. Encourage rotating junior ICs under senior mentor.
- Scenario template (example):
  1. Inject synthetic 5xx across a subset of API gateways in staging.
 2. Trigger simulated autoscaler oscillation.
 3. Observe routing behavior and practice opening a bridge using the template.
- Success criteria: under 20 minutes to reach containment decision; message published within 10 minutes of bridge open.

Post-incident artifacts and fast postmortem template (to be published within 72 hours):
- Summary: one-paragraph incident summary, impact classification (P0/P1), customers affected.
- Timeline (table): minute-by-minute highlights (include link to evidence snapshots).
- Root cause hypothesis and supporting evidence.
- Corrective actions (owner + ETA).
- Preventative backlog items and prioritization recommendation.

SLO and escalation thresholds (example numbers):
- Objective: API 99.9% availability per week for hosted endpoints; 95th percentile latency < 300ms.
- Alert triggers: 5-minute error rate > 0.5% OR P99 latency > 1.5s for 3 consecutive checks => open bridge.
- Escalation: If open bridge does not show metric improvement within 20 minutes, IC requests escalation authority to authorize region failover.

Operational notes and caveats:
- Use the sandbox for practice; do not alter live production routing or customer quotas during rehearsals.
- When in doubt on wording, default to transparent, concise messaging with acknowledgment of customer impact and next-steps.
- Keep messages factual; avoid promises about timelines beyond initial ETA placeholders.

Maintenance and ownership:
- Document owner: engineering (oncall-and-incident-response squad).
- Review cadence: semi-annual review and after each P0 incident (owner updates document and reviewers comment).
- Sandbox maintenance: eng-sre owns refresh of sandbox assets and simulated alert templates every 6 months.

Appendix A — Quick command snippets (examples to capture data):
- Capture recent deployments:
  curl -s "https://deployments.internal/api/recent?service=SERVICE" > /tmp/deploys.json
- Collect GPU capacity snapshot (example CLI):
  rwdctl cluster capacity --cluster cluster-a --output json > /tmp/capacity.json

Appendix B — Post-incident checklist for Comms:
1. Confirm incident closure and root cause memo.
2. Draft public postmortem summary (non-sensitive) within 72h.
3. Coordinate customer callbacks for enterprise accounts if impact >1 hour.
